items.e: May the writer and the reader be strong and steadfast in the very ark which is the house which the author prepared for himself.I now begin to explain the Torah portion, Shemot; which opens the second Book of the Torah.

NOW THESE ARE. Our book opens with a vav because the end of Genesis relates that Joseph saw the children of the third generation (Genesis 50:23). Scripture notes that Joseph’s brothers were few in number when they descended to Egypt but that they were fruitful and multiplied there (Exodus 1:7).The word elleh (these) and el (these) are employed equally with the masculine and the feminine. We thus find, For all these abominations (ha-to’evot ha-el) (Leviticus 18:27) and then afterward, any of these abominations (ha-to’evot ha-elleh) (Lev. 18:29). We similarly read, unto these men (la-anashim ha-el) (Gen. 19:8); These four (arba’at elleh) were born to the giant (II Samuel 21:22); and what can I do this day for these (la-elleh) my daughters (Gen. 31:43). The same is the case with the word laz (that one). We thus find, that Shunamite (ha-shunammit ha-laz) (II Kings 4:25) and this young man (ha-na’ar ha-laz) (Zechariah 2:8). The fact that the word elleh is penultimately accented indicates that its heh is superfluous. It is like the heh of laylah (night) and the heh of nachlah (brook) in the Brook of (nachlah) Egypt (Numbers 34:5).

[THE NAMES OF.] Shem (name) is masculine. Its plural form is shemot (names), for the tav is used for both the masculine and the feminine. Compare, mekomot (places) and avot (fathers). The mem is similarly used as a masculine and feminine plural. Compare, nashim (women) and pilagshim (concubines). We also find some nouns employing both the tav and the mem in the plural forms. Compare, nefashim (souls) (Ezekiel 13:20) and nefashot (souls) (Ezek. 13:18). We similarly find, levavot (hearts) (II Chronicles 28:9) and levavim (hearts). Compare, al livvehen (upon their hearts) (Nahum 2:8).[Into Egypt.] The heh of mitzrayemah (into Egypt) is in place of the word el (to). Compare, dotayenah (to Dothan) in nelekh dotayenah (let us go down to Dothan) (Gen. 37:16); and yerushalayemah (to Jerusalem) in and brought me in the vision of God to Jerusalem (Ezek. 8:3).
WITH JACOB. Et ya’akov means with Jacob. Compare, In that day the Lord made a covenant with (et) Abram (Gen. 15:18).

EVERY MAN CAME WITH HIS HOUSEHOLD. Beto (his household) refers to those who came out of his loins. The term bayit (house, household) in Scripture never refers to a wife. Every man came with his household (beto) is proof of this, for the wives of the tribes are not included in the seventy who descended into Egypt. Do not permit the verse and (the high priest shall) have made atonement for himself, and for his household (beto) (Lev. 16:18) to cause you any difficulty. For according to the plain meaning of the text, beto (his household) refers to his father’s house. Beto (his household) must be so interpreted because the high priest made three confessions on the Day of Atonement. The priest’s helpmate, who is his wife, is included in the term for himself . She is included with him because a husband and a wife make a “man.”

REUBEN. When a word beginning with a letter that is vocalized with a mobile sheva ( sheva na ), e.g., the zayin of Zevulun, has a bet, vav, kaf , or lamed prefixed to it, the prefix ideally should also be vocalized with a mobile sheva . However, due to the impossibility of sounding two mobile sheva’im in succession these prefixes are vocalized with a chirik rather than with a sheva . Hence if the word zevulun has a bet prefixed to it we say bi-zevulun (in Zebulun), If zevulun has a kaf or lamed prefixed to it we say ki-zevulun (like Zebulun) or li-zevulun (to Zebulun). However, if the word has a vav prefixed to it then it is vocalized with a shuruk rather than a chirik . We sound the vav as if it had an alef preceding it and pronounce the word u-zevulun (and Zebulun) for the word is sounded as if it were written alef vav plus zevulun . However, if we deal with a word whose first letter is a yod , an example being the name yehudah , then the yod is silent, for the yod is one of the quiescent letters. Compare, biyhudah (against Judah) in Let us go up against Judah (Isaiah 7:6) and kiyhudah (like Judah) and liyhudah (of Judah) in Of Judah, Nahshon (Num. 1:7). In the latter case the yod is silent and is not perceived or felt when the word is enunciated. The same is also the case when a vav is prefixed to the word yehudah . The word is pronounced viyhudah .The tribes are here listed in order of their births.

ISSACHAR. Because the two sins in yissachar (Issachar) are written in succession only one is sounded. Compare, the word machtzetzrim (did blow) (I Chron. 15:24), which is pronounced machtzerim . We do not find a similar case with regard to the sin in Scripture. It is customary for the Hebrews to pronounce a vav prefixed to the labials which are related to the vav , namely, the bet, mem, peh with an alef added to it, and to vocalize the vav with a shuruk . Compare, u-faru (and they shall be fruitful) in and they shall be fruitful and multiply (Jeremiah 23:3); and u-male’u (shall be full) in and the houses of the Egyptians shall he full of swarms of flies (Ex. 8:17). The word u-vinyamin (and Benjamin) is similar. Benjamin is listed before the children of the handmaidens because he was a son of one of Jacob’s wives.

DAN. Names are connected to each other in Scripture in six different ways. All of these styles are correct. One way of listing names is, Elam, and Asshur, and Arpachshad (Gen. 10:22). A second manner is, with carbuncles, purple, and richly woven work, and fine linen (Ezek. 27:16). A third way is, carnelian, topaz, and smaragd (Ex. 28:17). A fourth way is, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher . The fifth is, Myrrh, and aloes, and cassia (Psalms 45:9). The sixth way is, Adam, Seth, Enosh (I Chron. 1:1).

WERE. The word yehi (let it be) should have been vocalized like the word yirev (the multitude) in and the multitude of the burdens against him (II Chron. 24:27). However, since the heh is a guttural, the word yehi is vocalized with a segol beneath the first yod and the word is read yehi . Furthermore, the final yod of yehi should have been pronounced with a sounded sheva nach (a quiescent sheva ) as is the case with the word yirev . The word should thus have been pronounced yihey . However, because of the difficulty involved in the enunciation of the word in the aforementioned manner, the yod was silenced and we vocalized the heh with a chirik . Hence the word is pronounced yehi ( sheva beneath the yod ) as in, Behold, would it might be (yehi) according to thy word (Gen. 30:34), or yehi ( segol beneath the yod ), as in For He spoke, and it was (va-yehi) (Ps. 33:9). The accent is placed on the last syllable of yehi and a sheva is placed beneath its yod because the word is used often in conversation, as in So be (yehi khen) the Lord (Ex. 10:10). Therefore only this root and the root of va-yechi in And Jacob lived (Gen. 47: 28) are found to have an imperfect yod prefix vocalized with a sheva when conjugated in the kal . The reason for this is that two letters of the two roots va-yechi and va-yehi consist of the quiescent letters yod, heh , the root of one being heh, yod, heh and that of the other chet, yod, heh . Now since the yod and the heh are quiescent letters and are at times not pronounced at the end of a word, the yod prefix is vocalized with a shev a. We do not find any such other case in the kal .

THAT CAME OUT OF THE LOINS OF JACOB. Loins allude to the male organ which is located near the loins. It is similar to and Saul went to cover his feet (I Sam. 24:4).The offspring of Jacob who descended to Egypt really numbered sixty-nine, not including Jacob who should be counted first. The Pentateuch therefore first states et ya’akov (with Jacob), the meaning of which is as we have noted earlier. In the first listing of Jacob’s descendants in the Torah portion va-yiggash (then Judah came near unto him) (Gen. 44:18), Scripture states, And these are the names of the children of Israel who came unto Egypt, Jacob and his sons (Gen. 46:8). Thus with Jacob, all the souls of his sons and his daughters (descended from Jacob and Leah) were thirty and three (Gen. 46:15). The verse Thy fathers went down into Egypt with threescore and ten souls (Deuteronomy 10:22) is proof that Jacob is counted among the seventy, for Jacob had a soul. Similarly, Joseph and his two sons who were in Egypt are also included in the seventy.

AND JOSEPH DIED AND ALL THAT GENERATION. A father and his son comprise two generations. Proof of this is the fact that after Job’s fortune was changed for the better, he lived a hundred and forty years and saw four generations (Job 42:16). Furthermore, our sages tell us that there were ten generations from Adam to Noah and ten generations from Noah to Abraham (Abot 5:2, 3). Now the years of each of the aforementioned generations were different one from the other.
The meaning of And Joseph died is that he died in his greatness. Similarly, his brothers also did not see the evil days which followed.
[AND ALL THAT GENERATION.] This refers to the Egyptians. For Scripture goes on to note, Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph (v. 8).
AND THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL WERE FRUITFUL. They produced children as a tree produces fruit.

AND INCREASED ABUNDANTLY. Va-yishretzu (and increased abundantly) is similar to the word yishretzu (swarm) in Let the waters swarm (yishretzu) (Gen. 1:20). However, in the first instance the verb is independent. It is like the verbs went, sat, stood, and lay. In the second instance the verb is dependent upon something else. It is like the verbs ate, kept, and hired. We thus say, he ate the bread, he kept the thing, and he hired the donkey. The latter are called transitive verbs. Now yishretzu (swarm) in yishretzu ha-mayim (Let the waters swarm) is a transitive verb, while va-yishretzu (and increased abundantly) is an intransitive verb. Thus the root shin, resh, zadi is sometimes transitive and sometimes intransitive. It is like the root of the word shav which is at times intransitive as in and (God) will return (ve-shav) and gather (Deut. 30:3) and at times transitive, as in that then the Lord thy God will turn (ve-shav) thy captivity ( Ibid. ). It is possible that the word va-yishretzu alludes to the fact that the Israelite wives gave birth to twins and even more. I myself have seen the quadruplets that a women gave birth to. Physicians tell us that a woman can have as many as seven fetuses in her womb at one time.
AND MULTIPLIED. They did not die in proportion to that of a large nation.
AND WAXED EXCEEDINGLY MIGHTY. They had strong bones.

[EXCEEDINGLY.] The phrase bi-me’od me’od (exceedingly) indicates that there could not possibly have been any more of them. The bet of bi-me’od me’od is like the bet of ba-rishonah (first) in and they took their first journey (Num. 10:13), for we also encounter the term with out the bet in they shall set forth first (rishonah) (Num. 2:9).

AND THE LAND WAS FILLED WITH THEM. The land of Goshen, also known as the land of Rameses. Rameses is sounded with a quiescent sheva beneath the ayin , for the first sheva in Rameses, the sheva beneath the ayin which is connected to the resh , is called a sheva nach . The second sheva , the one beneath the mem , is called a sheva na (mobile sheva ) because the lips seem to begin to first move when it is uttered.

NOW THERE AROSE A NEW KING. This is to be taken literally without any embellishments. Scripture reads, and there arose (va-yakam) because the new king was not of the royal seed. It is like that my son hath stirred up (hekim) my servant to lie in wait against me (I Sam. 22:8).
AND HE SAID UNTO HIS PEOPLE. The Egyptians.

BEHOLD THE PEOPLE. The word am (people) is not in the construct with bene yisrael (the children of Israel). The term bene yisrael explains am and provides additional information concerning its meaning. It is like the words That I Am in the phrase I Am That I Am (Ex. 3:14) and the words Abraham and Isaac in the verse The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac did walk (Gen. 48:15).

FOR US. When the word mi-mennu (for us) is in the plural the books of the Babylonians adhere to the grammatical rule and always omit the dagesh in the nun in order to differentiate between mi-mennu in the plural and mi-mennu in Out of him (mi-mennu) shall come forth the cornerstone (Zech. 10:4). In the latter, nu is a third person singular suffix and has a dagesh placed in the nun in accordance with the grammatical rule. However, all the books coming out of the Land of Israel have a dagesh in the nun of mi-mennu both in the singular and in the plural because the nun of mi-menni (from me) in the singular has a dagesh despite the rule. For the nuns of ani (I) and necheni (hath led me) in the Lord hath led me (Gen. 24:27) do not receive a dagesh .Now the word min (from) is doubled, the nun of mi-menni receives a dagesh to make up for the missing nun of the second min , and the word is read as if written mi-menni . The nun of the first min is represented by the dagesh in the second mem of mi-menni and the nun of the suffix ni serves as if it were in the place of the one speaking. Similarly, the nun of mi-munnu in the plural, spelled mem mem nun nun vav (Gen. 23:6), receives a dagesh and is read as if written mi-mennu . The reason that the nun of mi-mennu (of him) in the singular receives a dagesh is to compensate for the swallowed heh , for it is only in a few instances when the verb yishmor (he will keep) is combined with a third person suffix that we say yishmero (he will keep him). The same is true of the word yikre’o (he shall be called) in whereby he shall be called (Jer. 23:6) and the word yirdefo (shall pursue him) in The enemy shall purse him (Hosea 8:3). The usual form of the third person suffix is yishmerehu (preserve him) (Ps. 41:8). Thus yishmero (he will keep him) is a shortened form. It is similar to hinnehu in and, behold, he (ve-hinnehu) was at his work (Jer. 18:3), in which hinnehu is a compound of hinneh (behold) and hu (he); and to ve-hinneh nitzav (and, lo he stood) (Num. 23:6). At other times an additional nun is added, as in yeshacharuneni (they will seek me earnestly) and yimtza’uneni (they will find me) in They will seek me earnestly, but they shall not find me (Proverbs 1:28). Similarly, the word tevarakhani (may bless me) in that thy soul may bless me (Gen. 27:19) is pronounced tevarekhanni because of the dagesh in the nun . We also find an extra nun in the word yekhabbdaneni (honoreth Me) in whoso offereth the sacrifice of thanksgiving honoreth Me (Ps. 50:23) and in the words yesovavenhu (He compassed him about), yevonanehu (He cared for him), and yitzrenhu (He kept him) (Deut. 32:10). At other times the third person heh suffix is swallowed by the nun , as in yishmerennu (kept it in) in and its owner hath not kept it in (Ex. 21:29).

COME (HAVAH). The word havah (give) in Give me my wife (Gen. 29:21) is in the masculine and as such is properly used there. It is similar to the word lekhah (come) in come, I pray thee with us . In the feminine we say havi , as in Bring (havi) the mantle that is upon thee (Ruth 3:15), and lekhi (go), as in Go and get thee in (I Kings 1:23). Now because these words are used often the masculine form is employed both as a plural and as a feminine singular. Scripture thus reads, Come (havah), let us go down (Gen. 11:7); Come (havah) I Pray thee, let me come in unto thee (Gen. 38:16). It is like Come (lekhah), let us make our father drink wine (Gen. 19:32).
LET US DEAL WISELY. Let us search for a wise way to prevent them from multiplying.

WITH THEM. The word lo (with them) is to be rendered, because of them. It is similar to the word li (of me) in say of me (Gen. 20:13).Note that all perfect and imperfect verbs imply a verbal noun. In other words, even though a noun derived from a verb is missing in the text it is implied in the verb. For example, ve-hinneh berakhta varekh (and, behold, thou hast blessed them altogether) (Num. 23:11) and And when He hath blessed, I cannot call it back (Num. 23:20), the meaning of which is: And when he hath blessed a blessing, I cannot call it back. The same is true of But in the multitude of counsellors they are established (Prov. 15:22). The complete version of the latter is: But in the multitude of counsellors, counsel is established. Similarly, when there befalleth us any war (v. 10) is to be interpreted as, when there befalleth us any accidents of war.Rabbi Merinus says that and get them out of the land means, and we will get us out of the land. He believes that Pharaoh said and get them out of the land so that Satan would not ensnare him in the utterances of his mouth. However, I see no need for this interpretation.

TASKMASTERS. Missim (taskmasters) is a plural. Its singular form is mas . This word is similar in form to pittim (pieces of bread) (Lev. 2:7) and pat (piece of bread) (Gen. 18:5). The word comes from a stem whose second and third root letters are identical.
[TO AFFLICT THEM.] To cause the semen of the men to dry up.

STORE-CITIES. Miskenot means store-cities. Ha-sokhen (this steward) in unto this steward (Is. 22:15) and sokhenet (companion) in and be a companion for the king (I Kings 1:2) are similar. For the meaning of the latter verse is, let her be in charge of the king’s treasury so that no one will know that she lies in thy bosom.
RAAMSES. Has a pattach beneath the ayin and does not refer to the place where Israel dwelt.
BUT THE MORE THEY AFFLICTED THEM. Even though they were afflicted. THE MORE THEY MULTIPLIED. As they did in the days when they were not afflicted.

AND THE MORE THEY SPREAD ABROAD. They were fruitful and increased above and beyond the norm. Yifrotz (they spread abroad) is like poretz (breaketh) in And whoso breaketh through a fence (Ecclesiastes 10:8).

TO SERVE. Pharaoh devised many evils with which to afflict the Israelites. First he ordered them to do his work. When he saw that this did not diminish their greatly increasing numbers he gave permission to the Egyptians and their princes to work them harder than slaves are normally worked. The latter is, as Onkelos explains, the meaning of the term be-farekh (with rigor). It is totally wrong to employ the form perukhim (broken) in liturgical poetry. When Pharaoh saw that the above measures did not stop the Israelites from increasing, he called the midwives (v. 13), the ones who were in charge of all the other midwives, and commanded them to kill all the males that were born.

AND THEY MADE THEIR LIVES BITTER. It is known that the tav , in a majority of instances, is the sign of the feminine plural and the mem of the masculine plural. Compare, mo’adot (seasons) (II Chron. 8:13) and mo’adim (seasons) (Gen. 1:14). According to the Spanish scholars verbal forms are kept and do not drop any of their root letters. However, this is not the case with nouns. Nouns are only employed as found in Scripture, for the singular of mo’adot (seasons) is mo’ed , not mo’adah as the person who thinks he is so brilliant believes. The latter would maintain that the plural of makom (place) is mekomim and the singular of mekomot (places) is mekomah . Perhaps he will open his eyes and see that the plural of bekhor (first-born) is bekhorim , as in To Him that smote Egypt in their first-born (bekhorehem) (Ps. 136:10). However, we also encounter the form bekhorot (firstlings) in and the firstlings of thy herd (Deut. 14:23). Now, shall the singular of bekhorot be bekhorah ? The same is the case with levenim (bricks). Its singular is levenah , not leven .

[IN MORTAR AND IN BRICK.] To build houses and fences. They also had to plow, harvest, prune, and pick olives. This is the meaning of and in all manner of service in the field . Scripture then alludes to all the other types of work which Israel did to fulfill the needs of the Egyptians by the general term in all their service .

WHEREIN THEY MADE THEM SERVE. The word avedu (they made them serve) is to be read as if written twice. Our verse is to be read as if it were written: wherein they made them serve, they made them serve with rigor. When a verb from the root ayin, bet, dalet is not followed by a bet it refers to work performed by a slave. This is the meaning of avadatikha (I have served thee) (Gen. 30:26). However, when the verb is followed by a bet it has one of the following two meanings. It means for the sake of, as in va-ya’avod yisrael be-ishah (and Israel served for a wife) (Hos. 12:13). Its other meaning is illustrated by thou shalt not make him to serve (lo ta’avod bo) with rigor , which is like which hath not been wrought with (lo ubbad bah) (Deut. 21:3). Which may neither be plowed (lo ye’aved bo) (Deut. 21:4) is similar, for we find, And the land that was desolate shall be tilled (Ezek. 36:34). In a like manner Scripture reads, As with the lender, so with the borrower (nosheh vo) (Is. 24:2).

AND THE KING OF EGYPT SPOKE TO THE HEBREW MIDWIVES. These midwives were in charge of all the other midwives. For there can be no doubt that there were more than five hundred midwives. These two midwives were in charge of all the other midwives and saw to it that they gave a tax to the king from the money they collected for their services. I have seen such a practice in many places. The opinion that the two midwives were mother and daughter was handed down by tradition, for it is correct.

WHEN YE DO THE OFFICE OF A MIDWIFE TO THE HEBREW WOMEN. Whoever comes from the family of ever (Eber) is called a Hebrew. One is called a Hebrew because of his faith. Hence the children of Eber (Ever) in the father of all the children of Eber (Gen. 10:21) refers to those who came from the side ( ever ) of the river. The side of the river refers to one of the banks of the river.

[THE BIRTHSTOOL.] Ben Kuraish says that the alef of ovnayim (birthstool) is superfluous because ovnayim comes from the same root as banim (sons). The meaning of ovnayim is birthstool. Ovnayim is similar to afsayim (ankles) in waters that were to the ankles (Ezek. 47:3). In reality, however, ovnayim is similar to ba-ovnayim (at the wheel) and the alef is a root letter.
THEN YE SHALL KILL HIM. In secret so that it will not become known, because he was committing an act of violence.

[THEN SHE SHALL LIVE.] The word va-chayah (then she shall live) is irregular and presents a very difficult grammatical problem. The rules of grammar require va-chayetah because the heh of the root changes to a tav , as it does in the construct in the case of the word chayat (beast of) in and to every beast of the earth (Gen. 1:30). The reason for the change is that the heh and the tav are similar in appearance when written. The only difference between them is the extension of the dot that is within the heh . For the letter tav is first a heh . It is only when the dot is extended that it becomes a tav . However, the tav and the heh are pronounced completely differently. They also have different names. This proves that our form of the letters is the original Hebrew script.Generally speaking, the root of the word chai (lived) and the root of the word chayyim (life) are in doubt, for the grammarians have concluded that the root of the word chai (lived) in And Arpachshad lived (Gen. 11:12) is chet, yod, yod . The word tam (spent) in how that our money is all spent (Gen. 47:18) is similar, for it comes from the root tav, mem, mem . The grammarians also agree that the plural of the root chet, yod, yod is chayyim (life). However, in my opinion we are dealing with an irregular root. If this is not so let someone show me a case where this root is conjugated in the imperfect according to the paradigm of chet, gimel, gimel , namely, achog (I will celebrate), tachog (you will celebrate), yachog (he will celebrate), la-chog (to celebrate). If the root of chai were chet, yod, yod , it should be conjugated achoy, yachoy, la-choy in the imperfect or like sov (go about) or sobu (walk about) in Walk about Zion (Ps. 48:13) and sobbi (go about) in Go about the city (Is. 23:16). This is proof that the word chai comes from a root ending in a heh . The fact that we do not find the root of chai conjugated in any of the above-mentioned forms is proof that it belongs to those verbs whose stems end in a heh , for we say echeyeh (I will live), nichyeh (we will live), eheyeh (I will be), tiheyeh (you will be), yiheyeh (he will be), all of which come from the root heh, yod, heh . Now if this is the case it comes from the root chet, yod, heh and is like the word haya (was). The fact that we find the word chai (lived) employed as a third person perfect in arpachshad chai (Arpachshad lived) (Gen. 11:12) does not disturb us. We are not bothered by the aforementioned even though it appears that chai comes from a double root. What forced me to come to this conclusion is the fact that I saw that there is no root in Hebrew that ends in a vav . The word shalev (at ease) (Job 16:12) does not disprove my contention. Its vav is in place of a heh , since the letters alef, heh, vav, yod interchange. Proof that what I say is correct is the word shalu (secure) in Wherefore are all they secure that deal treacherously (Job 12:1). For the root of shalu is shin, lamed, heh .I will now explain to you why a vav is never employed as a third letter of a root. The latter is so because the vav serves as a third person singular suffix, as in the words avdo va-amato (his man-servant nor his maid-servant) (Ex. 20:14). The vav also serves as the sign of the plural, as in peru u-revu (be fruitful and multiply) (Gen. 1:22). There are also superfluous vavs , as in beno be’or (the son of Beor) (Num. 24:3). Now if the vav was also used as the final letter of a root it would be confused with one of the three types of vavs that we have just mentioned, namely, the vav indicating a third person singular suffix, the vav indicating a plural, and the superfluous vav ; we could not then ascertain the meaning of the word. The same is also true of the yod . The yod cannot serve as the final letter of a stem because it is used as a first person singular suffix, as in the word yadi (my hand) (Gen. 42:37). It is also employed as a first person plural suffix, as in the word yadai (my hands) (Deut. 9:15). It is also the sign of the plural construct, as in yede (the hands of) in The hands of women full of compassion (Lamentations 4:10). It is used as the sign of the feminine imperative, as in de’i and re’i (know and consider) (I Sam. 25:17). It is used to indicate relationship, as in ha-ivri o ha-ivriyah (a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman) (Deut. 15:22). The yod is also used superfluously in verbs, as in ha-magbihi (that is enthroned) (Ps. 113:5) and in le-hoshivi (that He may set him) (Ps. 113:8). It is used superfluously with nouns, as in beni atono (his ass’s colt) (Gen. 49:11) and also with particles, as in zulati (save) (Deut. 1:36) and minni ephrayim (out of Ephraim) (Judges 5:14). For these reasons the yod is not employed as a final root letter lest it be confused with one of the above-noted yods . Therefore I maintain that the word va-chayah (then shall she live) is irregular and is a variant of va-chayetah . It belongs, as I have already explained, in the family of verbs ending in a heh .
BUT THE MIDWIVES FEARED GOD. The alef in va-tirena (feared) is not sounded lest the verb be thought to come from the root resh, alef, heh .
BUT SAVED. Even more than at first, they now worked with all of their strength to save the children. Otherwise what need was there for Scripture to be so verbose?

AND THE KING OF EGYPT CALLED FOR THE MIDWIVES, AND SAID UNTO THEM. You deserve to die because you have not obeyed my command. There is no difference in the form of the word va-tomarnah (said) in which the vav is vocalized with a pattach when it is in the third person perfect, like the word va-tokhalnah (did eat) in And the ill-favoured, and lean-fleshed kine did eat (Gen. 41:4), and when it is used as a second person perfect. The meaning of our verse is: Why have ye done this thing and preserved the man-children alive?

AND THE MIDWIVES SAID UNTO PHARAOH. We have not violated your command because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women; they have greater vitality. The yod of the word chayot (lively) in For they are lively does not have a dagesh . This is correct Hebrew usage. Compare, davot (ill), ravot (satiated), and alot (giving suck) in the flocks and herds giving suck are a care to me (Gen. 33:13). However, the yod in the word chayyim does receive a dagesh because chayyim is an adjective. Compare, ve-nitpesem chayyim (we shall take them alive) (II Kings 7:12) in which the yod in chayyim (alive) is like the yod of ha-ivriyyim (the Hebrews) in the God of the Hebrews (Ex. 3:18). The word chayyim (life) also receives a dagesh when it is a noun, as in etz chayyim (a tree of life) (Prov. 3:18). Similarly, the tzadi of tzitzim (flowers) in and open flowers (II Kings 6:18) receives a dagesh .

AND ARE DELIVERED. Ve-yaladu (and are delivered) is a feminine perfect. The third person perfect has the same form in the masculine and the feminine. Compare, tavu (did spin) (Ex. 35:25) and tzave’u (did service) (Ex. 38:8).

AND GOD DEALT WELL. When a root begins with a yod , the yod does not always drop out when the verb is conjugated, The word va-yetev (dealt well) is an example. At other times a vav is substituted for the yod , as in va-yoshev (He maketh to dwell) in And there He maketh the hungry to dwell (Ps. 107:36). The root of va-yoshev is yod, shin, bet , as the root of va-yetev is yod, tet, bet . And God dealt well is explained by what follows next, i.e., He (God) made them houses . The meaning of He made them houses is similar to that the Lord make thee a house (II Sam. 7:11).

AND IT CAME TO PASS, BECAUSE THE MIDWIVES FEARED GOD. Because the midwives did not fear the king of Egypt but feared the Lord, the Lord dealt well with them. Note that the verb yare’u (feared) is neither transitive nor intransitive, because its meaning is, to be afraid of someone. Hence the correct way of saying “feared the Lord” would be yare’u me’et Adonai . Obadiah used a short form when he said, yare et Adonai (fear the Lord) (I Kings 18:12). It is for this reason that the word nora (revered) does not come in the nifal form as the words nolad (was born) (I Chron. 2:3), nishbar (broken) (Ps. 51:19), and ve-nidkeh (and contrite) ( Ibid. ) do. The intelligent will understand why.

AND PHARAOH CHARGED. All who occupy the throne of Egypt are called Pharaoh in the Egyptian language. Scripture does not relate the name of this Pharaoh as it does in the case of Pharaoh-neco (Jer. 46:2) who was so called in the tongue of his people. The same is the case with Pharaoh Hophra (Jer. 44:30).
THAT IS BORN. Ha-yillod (that is born) is an adjective. It is like gibbor (warrior) and shikkor (drunk).
AND THERE WENT. Because of their great number the Israelites lived in many cities. All of the latter were called the land of Rameses. Perhaps this woman was in another city.

A DAUGHTER OF LEVI. Son of Israel. She was the sister of his father.The person who says that wheat sown in another field will succeed, while wheat planted in the same field will not, does not speak the truth. The main reason that close relatives are forbidden to have sexual relations with each other is to sanctify Israel.

AND THE WOMAN CONCEIVED. There is no doubt that Aaron was older than Moses. Our sages similarly received a tradition that Puah and Miriam are one and the same person. It is also written, And his sister stood afar off (v. 4).Now we know that the four hundred-year period which ended in Israel’s redemption started with the day that Isaac was born, for Isaac alone is considered to be Abraham’s seed. Now Isaac was sixty years old when he begot Jacob, and Jacob was eighty-five years old when he begot Reuben, and one hundred and thirty years old when he descended into Egypt. If we add the sixty years of Isaac to the one hundred and thirty of Jacob we come up with a hundred and ninety years. We are thus left with two hundred and ten years. We then subtract the seventy years that Joseph lived afterwards and we are left with one hundred and forty years. Now Levi was forty-three years old when he came down to Egypt and he outlived Joseph by twenty-two years. Thus one hundred and eighteen years are left. For the verse states, So Joseph died, being a hundred and ten years old (Gen. 50:26). Now when did the new king reign? For how many years did the Israelites build the store-cities? Behold close to the birth of Moses it was decreed that all male children be put to death.Ben Zuta says whoever relates a story will not out of respect mention the most honored first. Therefore when Scripture states, and she (Jochebed) bore unto Amram Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister (Num. 26:59), it indicates that Miriam was the youngest. Now the “blind one” (Ben Zuta) forgot Shem, Ham, and Japheth, concerning whom it is written, and Noah begot Shem, Ham and Japheth (Gen. 5:32). Now Japheth was the eldest of the three. Furthermore, Scripture states, There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife (Gen. 49:31) even though Sarah was buried in the cave of Machpelah thirty-eight years before Abraham was interred there. Note that the nun is often dropped or is swallowed by a dagesh when it is the first root letter of a verb, as in the case of the nun of gesh in gesh holah (stand back) (Gen. 19:9) and va-yiggash (came near) in Then Judah came near unto him (Gen. 44:18). The nun is also dropped when it serves as the middle letter of a root, as in the case of af (anger) in And anger also went up against Israel (Ps. 78:21). Observe, the middle nun is swallowed. Therefore the peh of appo (his wrath) in that his wrath was kindled (Gen. 39:19) and the peh of appekah (thine anger) in Thine anger is turned away (Is. 12:1) receive a dagesh . The same is true of the nun of the root nun, tav, nun in the word titti (that I give) (Gen. 29:19), for titti is like tinti because its final tav is not a root letter. It is rather like the tavs of shivti (my downsitting) (Ps. 139:2), lekhti (when I went) (I Kings 2:8), and lidti (I delivered) (I Kings 3:18). It is also so at the end of the word, as in tet (to put) in to put the dread of thee (Deut. 2:25) and in titti (that I give) in that I give her to thee (Gen. 29:19). The same is true of nouns. The word for daughter ( bat ) should have been banah since the feminine of ben (son) is banah . However, in this case it would have been confused with the verb banah (hath built), as in that hath built (banah) a new house (Deut. 20:5). A tav was therefore substituted for the heh . It is similar to givirah (lady) and geveret (lady) as well as to atarah (crown) and ateret (crown) in which we find both the construct and the absolute forms used in the absolute. Compare, ateret (crown of) in A crown of glory (Prov. 4:7). It should be noted that the nun was also dropped for the sake of easing the pronunciation of the word. Hence the word is enunciated bat (daughter). The word bitto (his daughter) in Rachel his daughter (Gen. 29:6) is similar to the word amitto (his truth) which is the word emet (truth) with the third person pronominal suffix. Compare, chasdo va-amitto (His mercy and His truth) (Gen. 24:27). Thus the tav is the sign of the feminine and the nun is swallowed up. The plural of truth is emunot , and not amitot or amitiyot . Similarly, the plural of daughters is banot , not batot or battim .

AND THE WOMAN CONCEIVED. Scripture does not mention the birth of Miriam and Aaron because there was nothing special about their birth.When the word tov (good) is used with reference to a mature man it probably refers to the soul, as in “good with the Lord and good with man.” Or it may refer to the eye, as in a bountiful (tov) eye (Prov. 22:9). It may also refer to the body or its form, as in “of good form, and good to look upon.” However, because we find it used with regard to a child, viz., that he was a goodly (tov) child , we can only explain it as referring to the child’s form, that he was better than all who are born.

THREE MONTHS. Some say that Moses was born in the seventh month following his conception. However, this interpretation like so many others is Midrashic, for the Egyptians had no way of determining when the woman conceived. In my opinion Scripture relates the months that she was able to hide the child since it is impossible for anyone to predict when a women will give birth. It is also far-fetched to say that Moses was born in the seventh month following conception because those so born are undersized. Those born in the eleventh month are healthier and live longer, as most children are born close to the ninth month. One who knows the time of conception is able to ascertain the time of birth, and one who knows the time of birth can ascertain the time of conception. This was established by the ancients. I myself have tried it five times. For the degree and place of the moon and its constellation at the moment of conception is also the degree of the constellation that flowers at the moment of begetting The degree which flowers at the moment of impregnation will also be the degree at which the moon will be found at the time of birth. Now the time set aside for carrying a child is two hundred and fifty nine and a third days. The median time for pregnancy is two hundred and seventy-three days. The maximum time for being with child is two hundred and eighty-seven days. Those learned in astrology will admit this. The birth of the tribes does not refute this, because the order of their listing is no proof that they were born prematurely. We find many such instances in the Torah. It is therefore possible that Rachel gave her handmaid to Jacob when Simeon was born, that Issachar was born before Asher, and that Dinah was Zebulun’s twin. Hence the phrase and afterwards in and afterwards she bore a daughter (Gen. 30:21) is similar to And after that came forth his brother (Gen. 25:26). For and she conceived is not mentioned for each one. Also, And it came to pass, when the seasons were come about (I Sam. 1:20) refers to three seasons.

[HIDE HIM.] The tzadi of hatzefino (hide him), like the kof in the word yikkrekh (happen to thee) in there shall no punishment happen to thee (I Sam. 28:10), receives a dagesh so that these words may be clearly pronounced. The peh in hatzefino should have received a dagesh . However, it does not because the tzadi is vocalized with a mobile sheva. Hatzefino is a hifil infinitive. There is no reason to speculate as to why Jochebed did not hide him for a longer period of time. Perhaps the Egyptian neighbors heard his voice, for the Hebrews were not the only inhabitants of the land of Rameses. For it is written, but every women shall ask of her neighbor (Ex. 3:22).
[AN ARK OF BULRUSHES.] The words tevat gome (an ark of bulrushes) are penultimately accented because the cantillical note is placed on the first syllable of the word gome (bulrushes).

AND DAUBED IT. The heh of va-tachmerah (and daubed it) is silent. It is like the heh of the word lah (it) in and called it (lah) Nobah, after his own name (Num. 32:42). The word va-tachmerah (and daubed it) is derived from the word ba-chemar (with slime). Chemar (slime) is a red sticky clay which is found in the Land of Israel. The word chemar (slime) in full of slime pits (Gen. 14:10) is similar. This substance is called al chamara in Arabic. Jochebed did this for she said, “Let me not look upon the death of the child.” Perhaps the sister of Moses prophesied that she do this. God’s thoughts are very deep. Who can know His secrets? By Him alone are actions weighed. Perhaps God arranged things so that Moses would grow up in a royal house and his spirit would thereby be exalted through learning and practice. He would thus not possess a base spirit habituated to being in the house of slaves. Do you not see that Moses killed an Egyptian because the latter committed an act of violence and that he saved the daughters of Midian from the shepherds because they were acting violently in trying to water their flocks with the water which the women had drawn? One more thing: had Moses grown up among his brothers and had they known him from his youth they would not have feared him because they would have considered him as one of themselves.
IN THE FLAGS ( BA-SUF ). Compare, The reeds and flags (va-suf) shall wither (Is. 19:6). Suf refers to a plant that grows in the Nile.

AND HIS SISTER STOOD AFAR OFF. The word va-tetatzav (stood) is irregular because a missing silent letter has been substituted for a yod between the two tavs .Rabbi Moses Ha-Kohen says that a tav is suffixed to the words laredet (to descend) and la-geshet (to approach) because the first root letter of these words is missing. That is also the case with the word la-da’at (to know). This word is vocalized with a pattach because the ayin is a guttural. Now in the word le-de’ah (to know) the tav was changed to a heh , as in the case of the word tenah (rehearsed) in Whose majesty is rehearsed above the heavens (Ps. 8:2).
AND THE DAUGHTER OF PHARAOH CAME DOWN. From her palace.

TO BATHE IN THE RIVER. As was the custom of Egyptian women. Scripture notes that her maidens walked by the riverside — the meaning of yad (side, place) here is the same as that of yad (place) in Thou shalt have a place (Deut. 23:13) — because it goes on to say that she sent her handmaid (Amatah), who was one of the maidens, to fetch the ark. For a princess would not go among the flags, and the ark was placed far from the shore so that no one passing by would touch it. Furthermore, from a grammatical point of view the word amah (handmaid) cannot mean an arm, because its mem does not have a dagesh while the mem of ammah (cubit) in A cubit shall be the length thereof (Gen. 30:2) does. Additionally, ammah (cubit) in A cubit shall be the length thereof refers to a measure and not to an arm.

AND SHE OPENED IT, AND SAW IT. After stating, and saw it , Scripture goes on to elucidate further. Our verse is thus similar to And the house of David shall be as a godlike being, As the angel of the Lord before them (Zech. 12:8).

AND BEHOLD A BOY THAT WEPT. Moses’ limbs were as large as if he were a fully developed boy. Pharaoh’s daughter noticed that Moses was circumcised. She took pity on him because of his beauty. This is the meaning of that he was a goodly child .

THEN SAID…THAT SHE MAY NURSE. The first yod in roots whose first letter is a yod occasionally change, as evidenced in the word todi’a (you shall inform) which comes from the root yod, dalet, ayin and is spelled with a vav . In other cases a silent missing letter which is at times written and at times omitted is substituted for the yod and placed between the prefix and the middle root letter. This is the case with the word ve-tenek (that she may nurse) in that she may nurse the child for thee .
AND PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER SAID TO HER: GO. Lekhi (go) is like shevi (sit). These words are the imperative forms of va-yelekh (and he went) and va-yeshev (and he dwelt).

TAKE. Helikhi (take) is like heniki (nurse) because the roots yod, lamed, kaf and heh, lamed, kaf are two roots with one meaning. For the heh is not one of the implied vowel letters. Therefore the other heh is also like it. Furthermore, the alef and likewise the yod and the vav are found in the middle of a word at times written and at times silent, that is, pronounced but unwritten, but the heh is always visible when in the middle of a word. The words be-latehem (with their secret arts) (Ex. 7:22) and be-lahatehem (with their secret arts) (Ex. 7:11) are not, as I will explain, one and the same word.

AND PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER SAID. Saadiah Gaon says that helikhi (take) is a composite of two words. However, the Gaon spoke incorrectly. It is, as I have noted, one word following the paradigm of ve-henikehu (and nurse it) in and nurse it for me . The word is in the hifil . The Gaon also said that helikhi is a composite of the words he and lakh , the meaning of he being the same as he (behold) in Behold (heh), I will also bring thy way upon thy head (Ezek. 16:43). However, we do not find the form lekhi used in Scripture when a female is being addressed. The form employed by Scripture is lakh . Helikhi (take) is thus one word.

AND NURSED IT. Va-tenikehu comes from a root wherein the middle radical is dropped and the other two remain. Observe, we have in our verse two roots with one meaning. It is the same case with the word hetivi (make good) in make good melody (Is. 23:16) which is an imperative following the paradigm of helikhi (take) and the word hetivu (they have well) in they have well said all that they have spoken (Deut. 15:25), which is like hevi’u (they brought) in And they brought yet unto him (Ex. 36:3), which is a word that drops its middle root letter.

AND HE BECAME HER SON. This is similar to And these are the sons of Michal , and to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1). Zerubbabel was the son of Pedaiah the brother of Shealtiel (II Chron. 3:17-19). He is called the son of Shealtiel because Shealtiel raised him.

[MOSES.] Moshe (Moses) is a Hebrew form of an Egyptian name. Moses was called Monyos in Egyptian. The name is so written in a book on agriculture which was translated from Egyptian into Arabic. This is also recorded in the books of the Greek scholars. Perhaps the daughter of Pharaoh learned our language, or she asked some one for its Hebrew version. Do not be perplexed as to why moshe was not called mashuy , as nouns do not keep their forms as verbs do.

THAT HE WENT OUT UNTO HIS BRETHREN. The Egyptians, for he was in the king’s palace. One of his brethren means one of his family, as in for we are brethren (Gen. 13:6). Our clause is to be so understood because Scripture has already noted that the man was a Hebrew.
STRIVING. Nitzim (striving) is a nifal adjective. The complete form is nintzim (striving). Compare, nirim (seen).
TO HIM THAT DID WRONG. To him that acted violently.
SAYEST THOU TO KILL ME. Sayest thou in thy heart.
SURELY. Akhen (surely) means if so.

HEARD. The land of Midian was subservient to Pharaoh; hence Moses had to herd sheep and not live among people and be recognized. It was at the time that his youngest son was born that God told Moses that Pharaoh and his servants from whom he had fled were dead. Upon hearing this Moses said, and (God) delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh (Ex. 18:4), as Moses feared Pharaoh as long as Pharaoh lived. After noting and (Moses) dwelt in the land of Midian , Scripture goes back and explains why Moses dwelt in Midian. Moses first sat down before the specified well. It is like And Jacob went out from Beer-sheba and went to Haran (Gen. 28:10). After stating the aforementioned the Pentateuch backsteps and states, And he lighted upon the place , etc. (Gen. 28:11).

NOW THE PRIEST OF MIDIAN. The reference is to Jethro and not Reuel. The term kohen (priest) in Scripture refers to one who ministers either to the Lord or before an idol. That they may minister unto Me in the priest’s office (Ex. 28:41) and the priests of the Lord (Is. 61:6) are proof of this. Jethro, as I will explain, was a priest of the Lord.

AND THE SHEPHERDS CAME. The mem of va-yegareshum (and drove them away) has the same meaning as a nun . If va-yegareshum was spelled with a nun , the nun might be confused with a superfluous nun . Similarly, the word tzonam (their flock) is spelled with a mem so as not to combine two nuns .

AND WHEN THEY CAME TO REUEL THEIR FATHER. Reuel was their grandfather, while Jethro, who was also known as Hobab, was the father-in-law of Moses. This is evidenced in these verses: even from the children of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses (Judges 4:11); And Moses said unto Hobab, the son of Reuel the Midianite (Num. 10:29).
AND THEY SAID. They embellished what Moses had actually done. Or the water which they had drawn was insufficient for their flocks.

AND HE SAID UNTO HIS DAUGHTERS. A grandfather is often called a father. Examples of the aforementioned are: O God of my father Abraham (Gen. 32:9) and Nebuchadnezzar thy father (Daniel 5:18). Similarly, a grandson is called a son. Examples of the latter are: The daughters are my daughters, and the children are my children (Gen. 31:43) and And thou his son, O Belshazzar (Dan. 5:22).
AND HE SAID. Behold, Scripture is being brief. It does not mention that they called Moses, for we may logically infer that they did so.
CALL HIM. Kiren (call) is irregular, as it does not follow its normal paradigm.
AND MOSES WAS CONTENT. Perhaps Jethro the son of Reuel was then absent and is therefore not mentioned by Scripture.

AND SHE BORE A SON, AND HE CALLED HIS NAME GERSHOM; FOR HE SAID. He refers to Moses. Zipporah is the Cushite woman of whom Scripture later speaks. Do not believe what is written in the book called The History of Moses . I will give you a general rule: We should not rely on any book not written by prophets or by the sages who transcribed traditions passed on to them. We definitely should not rely on these books when they contradict reason. The same applies to The Book of Zeruhbabel, The Book of Eldad Ha-dani , and similar compositions.

THAT THE KING OF EGYPT DIED. Moses was now able to return to Egypt. The Israelites repented. Ezekiel notes that the Israelites worshipped the idols of Egypt. It was because of this that the Lord afflicted them. As a punishment for not serving God they served cruel masters.
AND GOD HEARD…[AND GOD REMEMBERED.] The meaning of and God remembered is that the time for their redemption had come.
AND GOD SAW. The violence which the Egyptians openly practiced.
AND GOD TOOK COGNIZANCE. Of what was done in secret.
